title: Psalm 27 in Elul
hookLine: said through the month before the High Holy Days: wait for the Lord, be strong

cards: Athletes have a preseason. Actors have rehearsals. Before a wedding there are weeks of fittings and planning and nerves.
Nobody walks into the big day cold. The Jewish year works the same way. Before the High Holy Days, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, comes a whole month of warming up.
In many communities it has its own sound, the shofar blown on weekday mornings, and its own psalm, said every day, often twice. That month is Elul.

teach.b: Elul is the last month of the Jewish year, right before Rosh Hashanah: a month for turning around, teshuvah, getting ready to stand before God. Tradition hears a hint in its four letters, aleph, lamed, vav, lamed.
They're the first letters of a line from the Song of Songs: ani le-dodi ve-dodi li, I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine. So Elul isn't only a time of fear. It's a time of closeness.
Every day of Elul, many communities add Psalm twenty-seven.
It opens with courage: "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?" An old midrash reads it as a map of the season ahead. My light: Rosh Hashanah.
My salvation: Yom Kippur. Later teachers added a third: when the psalm says God will hide me in His shelter, the Hebrew word comes from sukkah, so they heard Sukkot, the festival that comes after.
Read that way, the psalm walks through the whole holiday season. But it's honest, too. The middle gets shaky: hide not Your face from me; even if my father and mother leave me.
It isn't the voice of someone who has it all together.
Then the last line, the one Elul hangs on: "Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let thy heart take courage; yea, wait thou for the LORD."
Wait, be strong, wait again. Getting ready isn't about having answers. It's about staying, with courage, until the day comes.

how: From the start of Elul through the High Holy Day season, many communities add Psalm 27 to morning and afternoon or evening prayers, and Ashkenazi communities blow the shofar each weekday morning of Elul.

o: the shofar blast that ends Yom Kippur
the first month of the Jewish year

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine

s: Elul is only a month of fear and dread
its letters hint at 'I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine'. it's a month of closeness.

light for Rosh Hashanah, salvation for Yom Kippur; later teachers added shelter for Sukkot.

games.q: the High Holy Days are a month away and you feel completely unready. what does Psalm 27's last line say?
o: wait for the Lord; be strong, and let your heart take courage.
don't think about it until the day comes.
games.why: wait, be strong, and wait again. Elul is for getting ready with courage, not for having every answer.

practice: If you can, find Psalm twenty-seven and read all fourteen verses slowly, noticing where it's brave and where it trembles.

If not, sit with its first line, the Lord is my light, whom shall I fear, and let one fear come up; then with its last, wait, and be strong, staying beside that fear with a little courage, without solving it today.
If you pray, say the psalm as your prayer.
